indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.2.1.4: Recognize water and air as important natural resources
indicator.objective: Demonstrate the existence of air in the environment

skills.description: Recognise simple evidence that air exists
Know that air is all around us, even though we cannot see it

misconceptions: Air is nothing because we cannot see it.
A balloon is empty when deflated.
Wind is not air; it is a separate thing.

questions.stem: Can we see air?
hints: You breathe it but cannot see it.
questions.explanation: We cannot see air, but it is all around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is visible.

questions.stem: What do we use air for?
hints: You do it all the time.
You need it to stay alive.
questions.explanation: We use air to breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we only need air for blowing balloons.

questions.stem: How do you know air is in a balloon?
options: The balloon is big and hard
hints: What happens when you blow into a balloon?
questions.explanation: When a balloon is blown up, air fills it and makes it big and hard.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a balloon is empty when it is blown up.

questions.stem: Is there air in the classroom?
options: Only if the window is open
Only if the fan is on
questions.explanation: Yes, there is air in the classroom. Air is all around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air only comes from outside.

questions.stem: What do you need air for when you are playing?
hints: You get tired and breathe faster.
questions.explanation: You need air to breathe, especially when playing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they only need air when they are resting.

questions.stem: When you wave a piece of paper in front of your face, what do you feel?
questions.explanation: Waving paper moves the air around, and you can feel it on your face.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand that moving air creates a breeze.

questions.stem: What do we use to blow up a balloon?
questions.explanation: We use air from our lungs to blow up a balloon.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you use water to blow up a balloon.

questions.stem: Is there air outside your house?
questions.explanation: Yes, there is air everywhere outside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is only inside.

questions.stem: Ama switches on a fan. What does the fan do?
questions.explanation: The fan makes air move, which creates a breeze.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the fan creates new air.

questions.stem: Which of these uses air?
hints: It goes up in the sky.
questions.explanation: Flying a kite uses air (wind) to lift the kite.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the connection between kites and air.

questions.stem: What do you fill a balloon with to make it big?
questions.explanation: You fill a balloon with air to make it big.

questions.stem: Is air everywhere around us?
hints: Can you breathe anywhere in the room?
questions.explanation: Yes, air is everywhere around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is only in some places.

questions.stem: How can you show that air is inside a deflated balloon?
options: Squeeze the balloon and feel the air come out
questions.explanation: Squeezing a deflated balloon can push the air out, showing that air is inside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a deflated balloon has no air inside.

questions.stem: Why do we need air to breathe?
hints: What happens if you hold your breath?
questions.explanation: We need air to stay alive. Without air, we cannot breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we only need air for play.

questions.stem: Describe one way you can show that air exists.

criteria.description: Describes a valid activity (e.g., waving a paper, blowing a balloon, feeling the wind)
States what is observed (e.g., paper moves, balloon gets big)

hints: What happens when you wave a paper?
What happens when you blow up a balloon?
questions.explanation: Waving paper moves the air, and you can feel it. This shows that air exists.

questions.stem: What happens to a paper fan when you move it back and forth?
questions.explanation: Moving a paper fan pushes the air, creating a breeze.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the fan creates air.

questions.stem: Why can we not see air?
questions.explanation: Air is transparent and colourless, so we cannot see it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is invisible because it doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Ama says 'A balloon that is not blown up has no air in it.' Why is she wrong?
options: Because the balloon is still there
Because the balloon is actually full of air even when not blown up
Because the balloon is made of air
hints: Is there space inside the balloon?
Does the balloon look completely flat?
questions.explanation: Even a balloon that is not blown up has some air inside it. Air is all around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a deflated balloon is completely empty.

questions.stem: Demonstrate to your teacher one way to show that air exists (e.g., blowing a balloon, waving a paper, or using a fan).

criteria.description: Explains what they observed to show air is present

hints: What can you do with a balloon?
questions.explanation: This tests the practical demonstration of air's existence.

questions.stem: Write two ways we use air in our daily lives.

criteria.description: Names one use (e.g., breathing, blowing balloons, flying kites)

hints: What do you do to stay alive?
What do you blow into a balloon?
questions.explanation: We use air for breathing, flying kites, and blowing up balloons.
